cards.q: What are the Zipf sampler and mulberry32, and why does the suite use them?
cards.easy: Zipf is a heavy tailed distribution where the rank r item appears with weight 1/r^s, which mimics page popularity: a few pages get most edits and a long tail gets one each. mulberry32 is a tiny seeded random number generator, so every test stream is identical on every run.
cards.deep: zipf(n, s, rand) builds the cumulative distribution of 1/(i + 1)^s over n ranks, normalizes it, and samples by drawing u in [0, 1) and binary searching the CDF, so each draw is O(log n) after O(n) setup. Streams use s = 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 over 20,000 to 50,000 keys, which produce both heavy items above N/k (needed so the Space-Saving test is not vacuous, and the test asserts heavy > 0) and a long tail of rare keys that collide in Count-Min. mulberry32 keeps a 32 bit state, adds 0x6D2B79F5 each call, and mixes with xor shifts and Math.imul to return a float in [0, 1); it is fast and good enough for tests, though not cryptographic. Seeding means a failing assertion reproduces bit for bit, and the probabilistic tests were sized (3 SE, share below delta) so a correct implementation passes with near certainty.

cards.q: How does CI run the suite, and why is there no install step?
cards.easy: GitHub Actions runs node --test on Node 22 and Node 24 for every push to main and every pull request. There is nothing to install, because the sketch and helper modules have no third party dependencies.
cards.deep: The workflow is a matrix over node-version 22 and 24 with fail-fast off, checkout, setup-node, then node --test tests/*.test.mjs. The comment in the workflow says the missing install step is deliberate: it proves on a clean runner that the analytic modules need nothing beyond the runtime. node:test and node:assert/strict are built in, and the modules are plain ES modules, so the same files load in the browser and in Node. Pure modules mean the tests import exactly what the page runs, with no mocks for DOM or network. What CI does not cover: the DOM code in app.js, the canvas drawing, and the live stream, which were checked by hand and by the logged node runs.
evidence: repo:wikipedia-edit-stream/.github/workflows/ci.yml: node-version: ["22", "24"]

cards.q: What are the honest limitations of this project?
cards.easy: Count-Min barely collides with about 100 wikis, the live runs only used HyperLogLog's small range branch, exact counting is cheap at this rate, and the reconnect path was seen working once in the browser but never in a logged run.
cards.deep: Count-Min: 0 keys inflated in every run, so 12 of 12 within bound tests almost nothing. HyperLogLog: the switch to the raw estimator is at about 10,240 distinct editors, and the longest run reached 983, so the harmonic mean estimator ran only in the test suite. Scale: at about 30 events a second exact maps are cheap, which makes the comparison possible but means the sketches never had to earn their memory savings. Resume: Wikimedia dropped the stream once during browser testing and the page reconnected without a duplicate, but no logged run includes a reconnect. Evidence: three runs of 2 to 5 minutes, one sketch per run, so no coverage statistics. Other gaps: the bot flag misses unflagged automation, the delay tile includes clock offset, the node script that wrote the logs is not in the repository, and the write up's bot share (roughly a quarter) and Kafka offsets phrasing are looser than the logs and the docs.
evidence: repo:wikipedia-edit-stream/README.md: The Last-Event-ID resume path has been seen working once in the browser, with no duplicates, but no logged run has exercised it.
repo:wikipedia-edit-stream/README.md: HyperLogLog switches from linear counting to the raw estimator at about 10,240 distinct editors, which takes a long session to reach.

cards.q: What would you do next, and what breaks at 10 times and 100 times the event rate?
cards.easy: At 10 times the rate the page still works but the once a second audit and exact maps get heavy. At 100 times the browser's main thread and the exact counters fail first; the sketches would be fine. Next steps are moving ingestion off the main thread, sampling the exact side, and running many seeded sketches to measure coverage.
cards.deep: At about 330 events a second: JSON.parse and ingest compete with painting, the 5,000 id dedupe ring covers about 15 seconds instead of 150, and the page map reaches the 500,000 key reset in well under an hour. At about 3,300 a second: the main thread saturates, the O(k + P) audit becomes the bottleneck, and the exact sets dominate memory. Unaffected: HyperLogLog stays 4 KB and O(1) per event, Count-Min costs 4 hashes per event, Space-Saving O(log k). Changes: parse and sketch in a Web Worker or a server side keyed streaming job; keep exact counts on a sample or a bounded window; size dedupe by time, not count; switch to HLL++ with 64 bit hashes and 6 bit registers; raise k or key Count-Min by page so it actually collides. Experiments: 100 independently seeded HyperLogLogs on one stream to measure how often error falls inside one sigma (expect about 68%), and a long session that crosses 10,240 editors so the raw estimator runs live.
cards.say: At a hundred times the rate the sketches are fine; the main thread and the exact maps are what break. I'd move ingestion to a worker or a server job and keep exact counts on a sample. Then I'd run a hundred seeded HyperLogLogs side by side to measure coverage, which a single sketch can't.

cards.q: Why not just count exactly? Memory is cheap.
cards.easy: At 33 events a second exact counting is cheap, which is exactly why the page can check the sketches against it. Sketches matter when exact state grows without bound, has to merge across machines, or must exist per key and per time window.
cards.deep: Concede: here the exact Set and Maps fit easily, and the README says the sketches pay off only at volumes where exact counting does not. Defend with scaling: an exact distinct set grows linearly with distinct items, while HyperLogLog stays at 4 KB for any cardinality with about 1.6% error; Count-Min stays at 4 x 1,024 counters regardless of key count; Space-Saving stays at 200 counters. The stronger argument is mergeability: HyperLogLogs from many shards or hourly buckets combine by register wise max, so distinct counts over any union of partitions need no raw data. Per key per window state, for example distinct editors per page per minute, multiplies exact cost by keys times windows. The project's contribution is measured error on real traffic, so a team can decide whether 1.6% is acceptable before paying for exact state.
cards.say: At 33 events a second you're right, exact counting is trivial, and that is what makes the comparison possible. Sketches pay off when state is per key and per window, or has to merge across shards. HyperLogLog stays at 4 KB for any number of users and merges with a register max.
evidence: repo:wikipedia-edit-stream/README.md: Exact counting is affordable at about 30 events a second. That is what makes the comparison possible; the sketches pay off at volumes where it is not.

cards.q: Is 297 seconds of data enough to claim anything?
cards.easy: Not enough for a statistical claim about HyperLogLog's error rate, and the project does not make one. It is enough to catch implementation bugs, because the Space-Saving and Count-Min guarantees are deterministic and should never break even once.
cards.deep: Separate two kinds of claim. Deterministic: Space-Saving's count - error <= f <= count and Count-Min's no undercount must hold on every event, so 200 checks a second with 0 violations is a meaningful bug check, and a single violation would disprove the implementation. Statistical: one sketch observed over time gives correlated points and three runs give three draws, which cannot estimate coverage. The calibration claims rest on the offline suite: 100,000 distinct keys within 3 standard errors, and 200,000 event Zipf streams where Count-Min's share over epsilon N stays below delta and Space-Saving's bounds hold for every item. Admitted gaps: the raw HyperLogLog regime never ran live, and Count-Min had zero collisions. A stronger live study would run many independently seeded HyperLogLogs on the same stream and count how often each lands inside the one sigma band.
cards.say: For a statistical claim, no, and I don't make one from the live runs. The Space-Saving and Count-Min checks are deterministic, so zero violations over five minutes is a real bug check. The error calibration comes from the seeded test suite.
evidence: portfolio: A node script ran the same sketch code against the live stream for 297 seconds on October 8, 2026: 9,909 events at 33.3 a second.

cards.q: Isn't a browser dashboard a toy compared with a Kafka and Flink pipeline?
cards.easy: The deployment is small, but the problems are the ones a streaming pipeline has: resuming after a disconnect, duplicates, late events, event time versus processing time, and checking a summary against ground truth. The core logic is a pure, tested module that does not depend on the browser.
cards.deep: Concede: one consumer, no persistence, no partitioned parallelism, and tens of events a second. Defend: wiki/sketch.js has no DOM and is imported unchanged by the node:test suite and by the node verification script that wrote the logs, and CI runs the suite on Node 22 and 24 with no install step. The stream semantics map directly onto production concepts: Last-Event-ID is a committed consumer position, RecentIds is idempotent consumption under at least once delivery, the 2 second settle is a watermark, the late counter is a side output, and exact versus sketch is a shadow computation. Moving to Flink means swapping the transport and keyed state, not rethinking the algorithms.
cards.say: The deployment is small, I agree. But the sketch module has no browser code, it is the same file the tests and the logging script run, and the hard parts are the same as in Flink: resume, dedupe, late data and watermarks. Porting it means changing the transport, not the logic.

cards.q: You picked the run with the nicest HyperLogLog number for the headline.
cards.easy: The headline uses the longest run, and all three runs are published next to it, including the worst one at -1.2%. All three are inside the one sigma band.
cards.deep: Concede: the badge quotes +0.4%, and a reader skimming it sees the best looking figure. Defend: the write up states the other two runs in the next sentence (-0.3% and -1.2%), the README table lists all three with lengths and event counts, and the raw logs are committed in runs/. The longest run is the natural headline because it has the most data. Against the linear counting error at those counts (about 1.1%), the errors are 0.3, 1.1 and 0.3 standard errors, so even the worst run is ordinary. The honest framing is that three runs show no sign of a bug, not that the error is 0.4%.
cards.say: The headline is the longest run, and the other two are in the very next sentence, including minus 1.2%. All three logs are in the repo. What I claim from them is no sign of a bug, not a 0.4% error rate.

cards.q: Why write your own sketches instead of using Apache DataSketches or a Redis HyperLogLog?
cards.easy: In production I would use a maintained library. Here the goal was to implement each algorithm from its paper and verify it against its own guarantees, which a library call would hide.
cards.deep: Concede: DataSketches and Redis PFCOUNT are tested at scale, use better variants (HLL++ style bias correction, 6 bit registers, sparse modes), and would be the right call for a product. Defend: the page needs internals a library hides, such as the regime that produced each estimate, per item Space-Saving error terms for the lower and upper bounds, and the standard rather than conservative Count-Min update so the textbook bound applies. Writing them also forced the verification work: MurmurHash3 against SMHasher's value, rank edge cases, and Zipf property tests. Everything stays dependency free, so the same module runs in the browser and in CI without a build step. The risk of a home grown bug is exactly what the live audit and the test suite exist to catch.
cards.say: For a product I'd use DataSketches. Here I needed the internals: which regime produced the estimate, per item error terms, and the exact update rule the bound is proved for. Writing them is also what made me verify the hash against SMHasher.

cards.q: Your write up says Last-Event-ID carries Kafka offsets, but Wikimedia emits timestamps. Which is it?
cards.easy: Timestamps. The id names Kafka topic and partition positions, and Wikimedia fills them with timestamps because offsets are only meaningful inside one Kafka cluster and it runs several. The write up's wording is loose.
cards.deep: Concede: the portfolio text says the id carries the stream's Kafka offsets, and the Wikitech documentation says ids always use timestamps instead of offsets in the multi datacenter setup. The page's own method notes have it right: a JSON list of Kafka topic and partition positions, as observed a millisecond timestamp for the active datacenter's topic. Defend the design, which does not depend on the distinction: resuming by timestamp can replay events that share a millisecond, and the manual fallback rewinds 5 seconds on purpose, so dedupe on meta.id is required either way. The practical difference is precision: an offset resumes at exactly the next event, a timestamp resumes at a time and needs idempotent consumption to be exact.
cards.say: It's timestamps, and my write up should say positions rather than offsets. Wikimedia runs several Kafka clusters and offsets don't carry across them. The design doesn't depend on it, because I dedupe on event id either way.

cards.easy: A live page that watches every Wikipedia edit and answers three questions twice, once exactly and once with compact estimators, to check the estimators stay inside their promised error.
cards.deep: Lead with the question and the result, then one design decision and one honest limit. Keep jargon to the three sketch names, each with a one line gloss. The number to land is 986.9 against 983, with the 297 second, 9,909 event context.

It answers each question twice, exactly and with a compact estimator that uses a few kilobytes. On a five minute run the editor estimate was 986.9 against a true 983, within 0.4%. It shows I can build streaming code and check it against ground truth instead of assuming it works.

cards.q: Explain this project to me as if I were a staff engineer.
cards.easy: Pure sketch module, exact shadow state, deterministic guarantees audited every second, event time bins with a watermark, Last-Event-ID plus id dedupe, and two honest gaps.
cards.deep: A staff engineer wants the mechanism, the invariants, and where it is weak. Name the parameters, the audit, the watermark, the delivery contract, and the two places the live data did not stress the code.
cards.say: The core is a pure module: MurmurHash3, a p equals 12 HyperLogLog, a 4 by 1,024 Count-Min with the standard update so the textbook bound applies, and Space-Saving on an indexed min heap. Each runs beside exact state, and the deterministic guarantees are audited every second. Throughput is binned on event time with a 2 second watermark, because arrival bins called delivery clumps bursts. Delivery is at least once, so I resume with Last-Event-ID and dedupe on event id. The weak spots are that Count-Min never collided and the live runs stayed in linear counting.

cards.q: Explain this project to me as if I were a product manager.
cards.easy: Dashboards often show estimated numbers without saying how wrong they might be. This page shows the estimate, the true value, and the promised error side by side, live.
cards.deep: A PM cares about what the user sees and what decision it supports. Frame sketches as the cheap way large products count things, the error as a cost the product can choose, and the page as evidence for that choice. Mention the plain language design: every card leads with a plain question and hides the math behind a toggle.
cards.say: Big products count unique users and top items with shortcuts that use a tiny amount of memory and accept a small error. My page runs the shortcut and the exact count side by side on live Wikipedia edits, so you can see the error instead of trusting it. On a five minute run the unique editor estimate was 0.4% off. Every card asks a plain question first, like how many people are editing, and puts the math behind a link.
evidence: portfolio: HyperLogLog 986.9 vs 983 exact distinct editors (+0.4%, one sigma bound 1.6%)

cards.q: Give me the recruiter version in under 30 seconds.

cards.deep: Keep it to what was built, the tools, one number, and why it is relevant to data and ML engineering roles. No formulas.
cards.say: It's a live dashboard of every Wikipedia edit, in JavaScript, that checks three well known streaming algorithms against exact counts as the data arrives. On a five minute run of about ten thousand edits the unique editor estimate was within half a percent.
